\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\looseness=-1
\textbf{RQ1} (independent confusability effect): Yes, on RE. BCS independently explains ${\sim}$27\% of cross-batch accuracy variance on FewRel after controlling for count and centrality, replicating across three model scales. \textbf{RQ2} (degradation modes): Count reduces recall uniformly; confusability drives type substitution (IntraSub) that scales monotonically with BCS. The two dimensions interact with bounded magnitude on the linear scale.
\textbf{RQ3} (decomposition): Schema decomposition fails in practice due to routing ambiguity (RE) and merge amplification (NER/ED), though oracle routing confirms the dimensions are separable in principle (\S\ref{sec:sdgd}).

\looseness=-1
We hypothesize that near-neighbor types in embedding space activate overlapping LLM representations, producing type-substitution interference, consistent with ecological confusability \citep{baan-2023-ecological}. This mechanism is specific to type discrimination, explaining why BCS predicts RE accuracy but not NER F1, where errors concentrate in span boundary and missed-entity modes. The confusability signal applies to cross-domain schemas; same-domain schemas exhibit centrality confounding (\S\ref{sec:centrality_confound}).

\looseness=-1
For practitioners, reducing candidate types is the primary lever for NER; for RE, pre-computing SCS/BCS can flag high-risk schemas before deployment (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-domain}). Naive mitigations (renaming, few-shot) do not close the gap (Appendices~\ref{app:renaming},~\ref{sec:appendix_fewshot_bcs}). Architectures that avoid explicit merge (e.g., retrieval-based type selection) may circumvent the decomposition bottleneck. Direct confirmation of the hypothesized representational mechanism via probing or activation analysis remains future work.
